transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Title: Northbridge Payments x Redwood — Benchmark report walkthrough (latency/$) + methodology Q&A
Date: Jul 2, 2025
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood) — AE
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions Engineer
- Priya Desai (Northbridge Payments) — Director, Platform Engineering
- Michael Tran (Northbridge Payments) — ML Engineer
- Anna Becker (Northbridge Payments) — Security & Procurement

Auto Summary (draft)
- Redwood walked through the public benchmark landing page and explained the latency-per-dollar metric and supporting metrics (p50/p95 latency, throughput, $/1M tokens).
- Northbridge raised concerns about workload fit (their traffic is bursty, streaming chat + long context) and whether Redwood’s published numbers can be replicated.
- Redwood clarified methodology: prompt set v3 production mix, fixed concurrency bands, warmups, caching/batching policy as documented, and stability gates/variance reruns.
- Discussion on deployment options for EU: Hosted EU region vs Dedicated capacity for predictable p95 and data isolation; Private/VPC mentioned as future option.

Topics
- Interpreting latency/$ vs tokens/sec
- Fairness + “apples-to-apples” model comparisons
- Replication: manifests, Docker runner, and what a customer can reproduce
- Region variability (eu-west vs us-east) and p95 stability
- Security posture and data residency constraints

Action items (verbatim)
- Stephanie: email Northbridge the benchmark methodology link + FAQs + a 1-pager on “how to replicate” (by EOD Fri)
- Markus: share sample run manifest + CLI flags used for region sweep runner and explain stability gates (by Fri)
- Priya/Michael: provide token distribution targets and 2–3 sanitized prompts for PoC (next week)
- Anna: send Northbridge’s baseline security questionnaire + data retention requirements (next week)

Questions captured
- “Is caching on in your public numbers? If yes, what kind?”
- “If we run the same harness, will we see the same latency/$ within some confidence interval?”
- “How do you prevent cherry-picking regions, times, or prompt mixes?”
- “What happens to p95 when there’s noisy neighbors on Hosted?”


TRANSCRIPT

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Hi everyone, thanks for making the time. I’m Stephanie, account exec here at Redwood. Markus is with me, solutions engineering. The goal today is pretty straightforward: we’ll walk through the benchmark report live, how to read the numbers, and then we can spend the rest on methodology and whether it maps to your workload. Sound okay?

[00:16] Priya Desai: Yep, that’s what we want. We got forwarded the report internally and… there’s enthusiasm, but also skepticism.

[00:23] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s healthy.

[00:24] Markus Klein: Totally.

[00:25] Michael Tran: Yeah I’m the skeptic, I guess. Mostly around like, can we reproduce it and does it match our traffic.

[00:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. And Anna, anything specific you want to make sure we cover?

[00:35] Anna Becker: Data residency and basically if this becomes a procurement thing, what we’re buying. Hosted vs dedicated, and what logs you keep.

[00:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. We’ll touch that.

[00:44] Markus Klein: I’m gonna share my screen.

[00:49] Markus Klein: Okay, so this is the public landing page. You’ll see the interactive table—models down the left, regions across the top. The default view is “latency per dollar” which is basically milliseconds of end-to-end latency you get per dollar spent. Lower is better. There’s also a toggle for p50 and p95 latency, throughput, and cost per 1M tokens.

[01:12] Michael Tran: Wait “latency per dollar” is lower better? That’s a little unintuitive.

[01:17] Markus Klein: Yeah, fair. It’s one of those units where we debated the label. Think of it as: if you spend one dollar, how much waiting time do you buy. Less waiting per dollar is better. If you flip to “tokens per dollar,” higher would be better. We chose this because it maps to p95 latency + spend, but we keep the underlying metrics visible.

[01:35] Priya Desai: Do you expose tokens per second too?

[01:38] Markus Klein: We do, but we push people to look at p95 and cost, because raw tokens/sec can hide queueing, and it doesn’t capture user experience when concurrency goes up.

[01:48] Stephanie Nguyen: And, just to state the obvious: this is not a “fastest model ever” claim. It’s about production economics in specific workloads and regions with our runtime.

[01:57] Michael Tran: Okay. What’s the workload though. That’s the first thing.

[02:02] Markus Klein: Great question. If you click “Methodology,” there’s a summary, and then a full methodology doc. The short version: we use prompt set v3 “production mix,” which includes both prefill-heavy and decode-heavy requests. We run across a few context length buckets. We also run at defined concurrency levels, with warmups, and we do repeated runs with stability gates.

[02:27] Michael Tran: When you say “production mix,” is that your production? Or like some made-up mixture.

[02:33] Markus Klein: It’s a curated mix built by our Applied ML team based on aggregated patterns we see across customers, plus public eval prompts that are safe to share. It’s not one customer’s traffic. And we publish the exact distributions we used—token counts, prefill/decode ratios—so you can judge fit.

[02:52] Priya Desai: Our workload is mostly chat, streaming, and long context. Like, 8k to 16k input sometimes, then short outputs.

[03:01] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s prefill-heavy. The report includes a context-length filter. Let me flip to the 16k bucket.

[03:11] Markus Klein: (scrolling) Okay, now you see numbers change. You’ll also see that some models degrade more than others on long prefill. That’s why we include that filter.

[03:22] Michael Tran: Are these all on the same GPU type?

[03:25] Markus Klein: Within a region, we run on a standardized fleet configuration for that run series. We don’t mix instance types within the sweep. Across regions, GPU type can differ—so we call it out in the methodology, and we normalize cost based on our actual metered infrastructure costs.

[03:41] Michael Tran: So it’s “Redwood cost” not like AWS list price.

[03:45] Markus Klein: Correct. The metric is based on what you pay Redwood for tokens in Hosted, and for Dedicated we can translate to effective $/1M tokens based on the commit size. The public report is primarily Hosted pricing. We’re careful there.

[03:57] Stephanie Nguyen: For your side, we’d likely talk Dedicated if p95 and predictability is the priority. But the report is still useful to pick a model and region.

[04:08] Anna Becker: Dedicated meaning isolated hardware?

[04:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Dedicated capacity pool, yes—data isolation, predictable throughput, and we can align on an SLA.

[04:18] Priya Desai: Okay, keep going.

[04:21] Markus Klein: So here’s a specific example. If you pick, say, Model A vs Model B—(pause) sorry, the model names are showing. The key is: in eu-west, you’ll see p95 is stable within a band. We publish p95, not just p50.

[04:38] Michael Tran: But p95 can be gamed too. Like if you run it at low concurrency.

[04:42] Markus Klein: 100%. That’s why concurrency is explicit. We run at multiple concurrency bands—think 1, 8, 32, etc. And we show where the knee is.

[04:52] Priya Desai: Do you show all of those in the public table?

[04:55] Markus Klein: The table defaults to a “representative” concurrency, but you can expand to see the other bands, and the PDF has charts that show the curve. Also, we provide CSV/JSON export for the full dataset.

[05:08] Michael Tran: Export is huge, actually. Because I want to compare it to our internal harness.

[05:14] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[05:16] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s a common ask. We’ve got customers using the dataset to shortlist models, then they run their own prompts on a smaller pilot.

[05:25] Michael Tran: Okay, I’m going to be blunt: is caching enabled in these numbers?

[05:29] Markus Klein: Good blunt question. We have a documented caching policy. In the main benchmark runs we do not rely on cross-request semantic caching, but we do allow runtime-level optimizations like KV cache reuse *within* a request and continuous batching. Prefix caching is controlled; we call out exactly whether it’s on and under what conditions.

[05:49] Michael Tran: That’s kind of the whole thing, right. If you have prefix cache and your prompt set repeats, you win.

[05:55] Markus Klein: Agree. That’s why we avoid repeated prompts in the public prompt set and we randomize certain parts. And the dataset includes cache hit rate metrics; if you see suspiciously high hit rates, that’s a red flag. We also have reviewers on the Applied ML side who check for that.

[06:14] Priya Desai: So the point is it’s not “we turned on magic caching.”

[06:18] Markus Klein: Correct.

[06:19] Stephanie Nguyen: And legally we can’t, and don’t, claim that your workload will match ours 1:1. We try to be transparent so you can map it.

[06:29] Anna Becker: When you say “prompt set,” is that public?

[06:32] Markus Klein: Parts are public, parts are internal. The methodology describes the composition. The reason some prompts aren’t fully public is licensing / safety, but the distributions and tokenization stats are published.

[06:45] Michael Tran: That’s… okay. But for replication, it matters.

[06:50] Markus Klein: For replication, what we provide is: the harness code path, the runner container (Docker image), the run manifest schema, and the config knobs. You can run it with your own prompts and see relative differences.

[07:04] Michael Tran: I want to replicate *your* numbers.

[07:07] Markus Klein: You can get close, but I want to set expectations: you won’t reproduce the exact same p95 down to the millisecond because regions, fleet load, and internet conditions vary. What we aim for is reproducibility within a confidence interval, and we publish variance and stability checks.

[07:25] Priya Desai: What’s the interval?

[07:27] Markus Klein: For most runs, p95 variance across repeats needs to be under a threshold—think single-digit percent—otherwise it auto-reruns. If it stays noisy, we flag it as unstable and exclude it from headline charts.

[07:41] Michael Tran: That sounds like cherry-picking again: you exclude bad runs.

[07:45] Markus Klein: Fair concern. The exclusion rules are published. It’s not “bad results,” it’s “unstable measurements.” If the measurement is unstable, it’s misleading to present a single number. And we keep the raw logs internally for audit.

[07:59] Stephanie Nguyen: Also, we can show you in a PoC what the stability looks like for your workload. That’s honestly the point.

[08:07] Michael Tran: Okay. Another: are competitor baselines in here? I saw some mention in the blog.

[08:13] Stephanie Nguyen: In the public report we’re very careful. We sometimes provide contextual baselines where we can do apples-to-apples, but we avoid “Vendor X is slower” claims without full substantiation. On this page it’s mostly Redwood results.

[08:27] Markus Klein: Internally we look at other providers—like Bedrock endpoints, OpenAI, Fireworks, Together—just to sanity check. But latency paths differ, and pricing differs, so we do caveats.

[08:40] Priya Desai: Our leadership is comparing you to Bedrock because they already have AWS enterprise agreements.

[08:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, very common. What we see is: Bedrock is a good default for procurement, but when teams need tighter p95, or better unit cost at higher concurrency, or more control over model versions and rollouts, they come to us. Dedicated is often the deciding factor.

[09:04] Anna Becker: And if we needed VPC?

[09:06] Stephanie Nguyen: We have Private deployments too—VPC, and on-prem for regulated. For this use case, you’re asking EU residency and predictable performance; we can start with EU Hosted or Dedicated in EU. Private is an option if network isolation becomes mandatory.

[09:22] Michael Tran: So for this benchmark, did you run in EU? Which region?

[09:26] Markus Klein: Yes—eu-west. Also us-east and some APAC, depending on availability. The table shows which regions are included.

[09:36] Priya Desai: Our customers are in Germany and France mostly, so eu-west is relevant.

[09:42] Markus Klein: Good.

[09:44] Michael Tran: Here’s another fit question: our traffic is spiky. Like lunchtime spikes. Does this benchmark include burst behavior or just steady-state?

[09:52] Markus Klein: The benchmark is steady-state at fixed concurrency for measurement. Burst behavior is more about autoscaling and queueing. On Hosted, we have rate limits and scaling policies; on Dedicated, you control burst headroom. But it’s not a “burst test” per se.

[10:10] Priya Desai: Okay, but in production, p95 goes to hell during bursts.

[10:15] Markus Klein: Totally. What we usually do in PoC is run two scenarios: steady-state at target concurrency, and then a burst ramp test to observe queueing and tail behavior. That’s outside the public report but we can run it with you.

[10:28] Stephanie Nguyen: And to tie it back to purchase decision: if burst p95 is key, that’s an argument for Dedicated so you’re not sharing capacity.

[10:36] Anna Becker: Dedicated means you can guarantee the capacity in EU? Like, contractually.

[10:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, with a commit and SLA language. We’d size it based on tokens/sec, context length, and concurrency, and build in headroom.

[10:52] Michael Tran: I want to go back to how you compute latency/$ because that’s the headline. Is it like p95 latency divided by cost?

[10:59] Markus Klein: Close. It’s a normalized metric combining end-to-end latency components and effective cost per token. The exact formula is in the methodology. We also show the raw components so you can compute your own. We don’t hide it behind a black box.

[11:15] Michael Tran: Do you include network latency? Like from where.

[11:19] Markus Klein: The measurement is from the runner in-region, to avoid “my office Wi-Fi” variability. End-to-end includes request overhead but within a controlled network environment.

[11:31] Priya Desai: That’s good for isolating compute, but our clients are global.

[11:35] Markus Klein: Yes. For client latency, you care about distance + CDN/edge routing. That’s separate. We can provide region selection guidance and multi-region failover.

[11:48] Stephanie Nguyen: In your case it sounds like EU primary, and maybe US for some internal tools?

[11:53] Priya Desai: Possibly.

[11:55] Markus Klein: Also streaming. Michael, you mentioned streaming chat. The benchmark includes a non-streaming measurement by default, because streaming definitions vary—time-to-first-token vs time-to-last-token. We do have TTFT metrics in some internal charts.

[12:12] Michael Tran: That’s a big deal for us. TTFT is the KPI.

[12:16] Markus Klein: Understood. In PoC we can measure TTFT and steady decode rate. Publicly, we’re cautious because it’s easy to mislead. But it’s measurable.

[12:28] Priya Desai: Is your API OpenAI-compatible? Like can we drop in.

[12:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we have compatible endpoints and SDKs. We can cover that separately.

[12:37] Anna Becker: I want to understand logs. Are prompts stored?

[12:41] Stephanie Nguyen: By default, we don’t use your prompts for training. Logging is configurable; we have redaction options. For Dedicated/Private, we can align on retention and audit logs. There’s also enterprise controls like SSO/SAML, RBAC.

[12:55] Anna Becker: We’ll need that in writing.

[12:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. We’ll send our security packet.

[13:02] Markus Klein: Going back to the table—let me click into the “download dataset” action. This gives CSV and JSON. The JSON includes schema versioning and a changelog field.

[13:12] Michael Tran: Nice.

[13:14] Markus Klein: Each row includes: model ID, region, context bucket, concurrency, p50/p95, throughput, and computed latency/$ plus confidence notes.

[13:27] Michael Tran: Confidence notes?

[13:29] Markus Klein: Like “rerun_count=2” or “variance_flag=false.” Again, transparency.

[13:37] Priya Desai: Okay but how do I know you didn’t run it at 3am when nobody’s using the cluster.

[13:44] Markus Klein: Good callout. We reserve capacity for benchmark sweeps specifically to avoid noisy neighbors, and we run repeated sweeps at different times. We publish the run window. And internally we keep raw run manifests with timestamps.

[13:59] Michael Tran: So it’s not “on the same shared Hosted cluster as customers.”

[14:03] Markus Klein: The benchmark environment is controlled. Otherwise it’d be chaos. The point is to measure the runtime and region performance, not incidental traffic.

[14:13] Priya Desai: But then it doesn’t represent real Hosted.

[14:16] Markus Klein: It represents what Hosted can do under normal conditions, but yes, any shared system has variance. That’s why for strict SLOs we suggest Dedicated.

[14:27] Stephanie Nguyen: I’ll just underline: the benchmark is a starting point. The sales motion is: shortlist from benchmark, validate with your prompts, then decide Hosted vs Dedicated.

[14:38] Michael Tran: Okay. If we wanted to replicate, what do we need? Like literally.

[14:43] Markus Klein: We can give you a Docker image—pinned deps—plus a CLI command. You choose region, model, concurrency, and prompt set. It outputs a manifest JSON and result JSON. If you want to run against our public prompt set, we can provide the parts that are shareable and you can substitute your own for restricted pieces.

[15:05] Michael Tran: And we can run it from our VPC?

[15:08] Markus Klein: You can run the runner from wherever, but for clean comparison you’d run it in the same cloud region. We can help you spin a small runner instance in eu-west.

[15:21] Anna Becker: Depends on the prompts.

[15:34] Michael Tran: Another issue: Our prompts have a lot of repeated boilerplate, like policy text. Prefix caching could help, but it’s not in your benchmark. So your benchmark might understate your advantage.

[16:00] Priya Desai: Okay so the benchmark is conservative in that sense.

[16:03] Markus Klein: In that particular dimension, yes.

[16:20] Priya Desai: I’m looking at the p95 numbers here and they’re… lower than what I see with Bedrock for similar models. Why.

[16:52] Markus Klein: We use published/standard serving profiles for each model. If quantization is used, it’s documented. We avoid non-standard “lab-only” configs. Again: publishable, defensible.
